```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_highs <- requireNamespace("highs", quietly = TRUE)
```

multimod represents a linear optimization model as an abstract syntax tree
(AST) of sets, mappings, parameters, variables and equations, independent of
any modeling language. This vignette takes one small model through the main
operations: reading and translating, analyzing structure and redundancy,
rendering to LaTeX, exporting, and solving. Each step is a single call on the
same model object.

```{r setup}
library(multimod)
```

## A model

The package ships two example models. `example_models$toy` is a small
capacity-expansion LP built with the constructors: three technologies supply
two regions at least cost.

```{r toy}
toy <- example_models$toy
toy
```

## Reading and translating

`read_gmpl()` reads a GNU MathProg model, with its data section, from a file
or from text. The result is a multimod model of the same kind as `toy`.

```{r read-gmpl}
src <- c(
  "set REGION;",
  "set TECH;",
  "param Demand{r in REGION};",
  "param Cost{t in TECH};",
  "var gen{t in TECH, r in REGION} >= 0;",
  "minimize total: sum{t in TECH, r in REGION} Cost[t] * gen[t,r];",
  "s.t. meet{r in REGION}: sum{t in TECH} gen[t,r] >= Demand[r];",
  "data;",
  "set REGION := north south;",
  "set TECH := coal wind;",
  "param Demand := north 10 south 5;",
  "param Cost := coal 3 wind 1;",
  "end;"
)
m <- read_gmpl(src)
m
```

Any equation of the model renders to GAMS, JuMP and Pyomo:

```{r translate}
meet <- m$equations$meet
cat(as_gams(meet))
cat(as_jump(meet, model = m))
cat(as_pyomo(meet, model = m))
```

`read_gams()` reads the linear subset of GAMS in the same way. A single
equation can also be written as MathProg, GAMS or JuMP text with
`mm_equation()`, which resolves its names against the model's declarations:

```{r mm-equation}
cap <- mm_equation(
  toy,
  "eqCapTotal.. sum((tech, region), vCap(tech, region)) =l= 2000;",
  lang = "gams"
)
cat(as_gmpl(cap, model = toy))
```

## Structure and redundancy

`validate()` checks that every symbol an equation refers to is declared and
that the dimensions agree. `model_to_lp()` assembles the constraint matrix,
and `check_matrix_numbers()` reports the range of its coefficients, which
indicates how well scaled the problem is for a solver.

```{r statistics}
validate(toy)
lp <- model_to_lp(toy)
dim(lp$A)
chk <- check_matrix_numbers(lp, verbose = FALSE)
chk$summary[, c("section", "entries", "min_abs", "max_abs", "orders")]
```

Redundancy is easier to see on a larger model. `example_models$energyRt` holds
the energyRt energy system model, parsed from its GAMS source with data
attached. `analyze_parameter_redundancy()` measures how many of each
parameter's values repeat across a dimension, which is what folding removes,
and `trim_model()` marks the symbols that the data leaves unused:

```{r redundancy}
big <- example_models$energyRt$multimod
red <- analyze_parameter_redundancy(big, verbose = FALSE)
head(red[order(-red$orig_redundancy_pct),
         c("param_name", "orig_rows", "orig_unique", "orig_redundancy_pct")])

trimmed <- trim_model(big, verbose = FALSE)
get_trim_summary(trimmed, format = "data.frame")
```

The "Folding and trimming" article on the website applies both reductions and
shows that the optimum is unchanged.

## LaTeX

`as_latex()` renders any node as LaTeX math, and `write_latex()` writes the
whole model as a LaTeX document. The demand balance of `toy`:

```{r latex-src}
eq <- toy$equations$eqDemand
lhs <- as_latex(eq$lhs)
rhs <- as_latex(eq$rhs)
lhs
```

```{r latex-show, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# MathJax has no \bm; \boldsymbol is its equivalent
cat("$$", gsub("\\bm{", "\\boldsymbol{", paste(lhs, "\\ge", rhs), fixed = TRUE), "$$")
```

## Exporting

`write_gmpl()`, `write_jump()`, `write_pyomo()` and `write_gams()` render the
whole model in one language. Without a file they return the code; the
declarations, objective and constraints of `toy` in MathProg:

```{r export-code}
code <- write_gmpl(toy)
cat(code[13:27], sep = "\n")
```

`save_model()` stores the model and its data as a workspace of CSV, Arrow IPC
or Parquet files, which the generated JuMP and Pyomo code reads at run time.
`model_to_json()` serializes the structure for other tools.

```{r export-workspace}
ws <- tempfile("toy-")
toy <- save_model(toy, ws, format = "csv", verbose = FALSE)
list.files(ws, recursive = TRUE)

json <- model_to_json(toy)
substr(json, 1, 120)
```

## Solving

`solve_highs()` assembles the LP and solves it in R with the 'highs' package:

```{r solve, eval = has_highs}
result <- solve_highs(toy, attach = FALSE)
result$objective
```

`solve_gmpl()`, `solve_jump()` and `solve_pyomo()` solve the generated code
with GLPK, Julia or Python instead, and load the solution back into the
model.

## Further reading

The articles on the package website,
<https://optimal2050.github.io/multimod/r/>, cover each topic in detail:

- "Writing a model in R": the constructors, building `toy` step by step.
- "Solving and reading results": every solve route and its output.
- "Folding and trimming": the two reductions and their effect.
- "Two models from the field": the energyRt model and a published MathProg
  model, read and solved.
- "Model workspace and data", "Configuring solver paths", "LaTeX rendering".
